business.title: Electricity 2026: Transmission and distribution
business.desc:
South Africa's electricity sector is undergoing significant transformation as policy, regulatory and market reforms reshape the country's electricity supply landscape. The pace of change continues to accelerate, with developments across legislation, market design, transmission infrastructure, investment and technology reshaping the operating environment.
Creamer Media’s ‘Electricity 2026: Transmission and distribution – the current constraints’ report examines the policies, regulatory reforms, institutional restructuring and infrastructure investment shaping South Africa's evolving electricity sector, with a particular focus on the transmission and distribution constraints influencing the pace of electricity market reform and new generation development. The report also explores the expansion of the transmission network, the emergence of competitive electricity markets, growing private-sector participation, renewable-energy and energy storage developments, and the opportunities presented by localisation and the Just Energy Transition.
Although considerable progress has been made, challenges remain. Grid constraints, financing requirements, implementation capacity and regulatory certainty will influence the pace at which reforms translate into new investment, enhanced competition and improved electricity security.
Against this backdrop, South Africa's electricity sector is expected to remain characterised by ongoing policy, regulatory, infrastructure and market developments as the transformation of the electricity supply industry continues.

world.title: Time for retaliation: How to respond to Russian sabotage and subversion?
world.desc: A state that responds to every act of sabotage by arresting the perpetrator, repairing the damage and strengthening protection around the next potential target may be achieving law-enforcement successes while losing at the strategic level. The adversary retains the initiative: it chooses the time, place and method of attack and, when one intermediary is lost, can find another. That is why a question long avoided is increasingly returning to the Western debate over Russia’s hybrid warfare: does an effective response to sabotage require not only resilience and defence, but also retaliation? Not revenge, nor a mechanical application of the principle of an “eye for an eye”, but a system in which the decision to mount an operation increases the cost borne by its actual organiser.
